At the edge of the city, where the last apartment building gives up and becomes a field, there is a bench no one remembers placing.

It faces west.

Every evening, people sit there for different reasons. A runner stops to stretch one ankle. An old man brings a paper cup of tea and watches the sky change color. Teenagers sit shoulder to shoulder, pretending not to be afraid of the future. Once, a woman arrived carrying a suitcase, stayed until dark, and then left without it.

The bench has learned not to ask questions.

It has held breakups, sandwiches, feverish children, sleeping dogs, and the occasional moth circling a phone screen. It has listened to people make promises they would keep for three weeks and apologies they had rehearsed for three years. In winter, snow gathers on its back like a white shawl. In summer, ants march confidently across its armrests, carrying crumbs toward some destination no human has ever been invited to see.

The bench believes that most lives are made of almosts.

Almost calling. Almost leaving. Almost saying the true thing.

But it also knows that people are more persistent than they think. They return. They try again. They bring different shoes, different friends, different versions of themselves. The horizon does not change much, but no one who sits before it remains exactly the same.

Tonight, a child climbs onto the bench and points at the first star.

“That one,” she says.

Her father looks where she is pointing. He cannot see it yet, but he agrees.

“Yes,” he says. “That one.”

And because the sky is wide, and because darkness is patient, and because sometimes belief is simply another name for looking carefully, the star appears.
